summary: This standards-track document defines the Service Location Protocol, a scalable framework for discovering and selecting network services. With it, computers need less static configuration for network-based applications, which helps as machines become more portable.

plainLanguage.summary: The Service Location Protocol lets an application ask the network for a service by type and attributes. A service agent or directory agent can return a matching service address, reducing the need for static configuration.

questions: how to discover network services automatically
what is a slp directory agent
subtitle: Discover a network service by describing what you need, not by knowing its host name.

tldr.problem: Applications often need a network service without knowing which host provides it. Maintaining every service address by hand is inconvenient as computers and services change.
tldr.mechanism: A User Agent asks for a service type and matching attributes. It can multicast to Service Agents or query a Directory Agent that collects service registrations.
tldr.outcome: SLP provides service discovery for local and enterprise networks, not global Internet name resolution. RFC 2165 was later updated by RFC 2608 and RFC 2609.

today: RFC 2165 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 2608 and RFC 2609. The batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it.

sections.title: Finding a Service by Its Features
sections.content:
The Service Location Protocol (SLP) lets an application request a service without knowing the host name of the machine that provides it. The request names a service type and can include attributes that describe what the user needs.

SLP is a dynamic configuration mechanism for local and enterprise networks. It is not a global resolution system for the entire Internet. The service itself is accessed through a mechanism outside SLP.
sections.plainLanguage: An application can ask for a service by describing it instead of naming a computer. SLP is intended for services inside a local or enterprise network, not for finding services across the whole Internet.

sections.title: User, Service, and Directory Agents
sections.content:
A User Agent (UA) asks for service information. A Service Agent (SA) advertises one or more services. A Directory Agent (DA) collects registrations from Service Agents and provides a central place for User Agents to query.

A service type defines the expected attributes and behavior for a kind of service. A service is represented by a URL, and a predicate lets a request select services whose attributes match its conditions.
sections.plainLanguage: A user agent searches, and a service agent advertises what it offers. A directory agent can collect those advertisements so users can search one place.

sections.title: Searching and Registering Services
sections.content:
If a User Agent knows a Directory Agent, it sends a unicast request and receives a unicast reply. Without a known Directory Agent, it can multicast a request; Service Agents that can satisfy it respond, while agents with no matching information MUST NOT respond.

Service Agents register services with an available Directory Agent. Each registration has a lifetime and must be refreshed before it expires. When all matching services are needed, a User Agent repeats a multicast request with a list of previous responders so that only new responders reply.
sections.plainLanguage: A search can go directly to a directory agent or be sent to listening service agents. Service agents register their services with a lifetime, so an old advertisement eventually expires if it is not renewed.

sections.title: Using Scopes as Networks Grow
sections.content:
SLP describes three operating modes: multicast discovery without Directory Agents for a LAN; Directory Agents without scopes for a limited group of connected LANs; and Directory Agents with scopes for an internetworked campus.

A scope is a logical group of services, often based on administrative needs. A large campus should avoid unscoped Directory Agents because they attract all registrations and can become a scaling problem.
sections.plainLanguage: Small networks can search by multicast. Larger networks can add directory agents and group services into scopes so searches stay within the intended administrative area.

sections.title: Message Types and Transport
sections.content:
Every SLP message begins with a shared header containing its function, length, flags, language and transaction identifier. The RFC defines ten message types, including service requests, replies, registrations, deregistrations, attribute requests, and Directory Agent advertisements.

SLP requires both UDP and TCP. UDP carries ordinary requests and replies; TCP is used for bulk transfer when a response does not fit in a datagram. Agents initiate connections to the Service Location port.
sections.plainLanguage: Each message has a common header that identifies its purpose and lets a reply match its request. Short exchanges can use UDP, while large transfers can use TCP.

sections.title: Security and Status
sections.content:
SLP can authenticate registrations for protected scopes, helping protect their integrity. It does not provide confidentiality. The RFC says sites needing confidentiality should use another protection mechanism.

RFC 2165 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 2608 and RFC 2609. Read those later documents alongside this version.
sections.plainLanguage: Protected scopes can check whether a service agent is authorized to register information, but SLP does not keep messages secret. RFC 2608 and RFC 2609 later updated this specification.
